title: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits

learn.hook: The first computers filled whole rooms with glowing vacuum tubes. Today, a phone made in Noida packs billions of semiconductor devices into a chip smaller than a fingernail.
points: Early electronics used vacuum tubes (valves) such as the vacuum diode and triode, in which electrons flowed through vacuum from a heated cathode.
Semiconductor (solid-state) devices replaced them: they are small, use little power, run at low voltages, are reliable and long-lived, and need no heated filament.
Classification by resistivity ρ: metals (10⁻² to 10⁻⁸ Ω m), semiconductors (10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m) and insulators (10¹¹ to 10¹⁹ Ω m).
Elemental semiconductors: silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge).
Compound semiconductors: inorganic ones like GaAs, CdS, CdSe, InP, and organic ones like anthracene and conducting polymers.

example.q: A material has a resistivity of 10² Ω m. Classify it.
steps: Metals: 10⁻² to 10⁻⁸ Ω m
Insulators: 10¹¹ to 10¹⁹ Ω m
10² Ω m lies in the semiconductor range (10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m)

learn.reallife: India's Semiconductor Mission is setting up chip fabrication and assembly units in Gujarat and Assam, building on the solid-state revolution that began with the transistor.

learn.hook: A single atom has sharp energy levels. Pack billions of atoms into a crystal and those levels smear into bands. The gap between bands decides whether a solid conducts.
points: In a crystal, the energy levels of neighbouring atoms overlap and split into many closely spaced levels, forming energy bands.
The valence band holds the valence electrons; the conduction band above it is where electrons can move freely. Between them is the forbidden energy gap Eg.
Metals: the conduction band is partly filled, or the valence and conduction bands overlap, so electrons move easily.
Insulators: Eg is large (more than about 3 eV), so almost no electrons reach the conduction band.
Semiconductors: Eg is small (Si about 1.1 eV, Ge about 0.7 eV), so at room temperature some electrons jump across and conduct.

example.q: Silicon has Eg ≈ 1.1 eV and diamond Eg ≈ 6 eV (much more than 3 eV). Which conducts at room temperature?
steps: Room-temperature thermal energy can lift a few electrons across a 1.1 eV gap.
It cannot bridge a 6 eV gap.
So silicon conducts a little; diamond acts as an insulator.
example.answer: Silicon (a semiconductor); diamond is an insulator

learn.reallife: Solar cells on rooftops in Rajasthan use silicon because its band gap of about 1.1 eV lets sunlight photons lift electrons into the conduction band.

revise.summary: In a crystal, atomic levels spread into energy bands: a valence band, a conduction band and a forbidden gap Eg between them. Metals have overlapping or partly filled bands, insulators have Eg > 3 eV, and semiconductors have small gaps (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV).

learn.hook: A perfect, pure silicon crystal is nearly an insulator when cold. Warm it up and it starts conducting with two kinds of charge carriers, one of which is just an empty space.
points: In Si and Ge, each atom forms four covalent bonds with its four neighbours, sharing electron pairs in a tetrahedral lattice.
Thermal energy breaks some bonds: each freed electron leaves behind a vacancy called a hole, which behaves like a positive charge +e. Electrons and holes are created in pairs.
In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, the number density of free electrons equals that of holes: ne = nh = ni.
Under an applied field, electrons move one way and holes the other; the total current I = Ie + Ih.
At 0 K all bonds are intact and the semiconductor is an insulator. As temperature rises, more pairs form and conductivity increases.

example.q: A pure germanium sample has ni = 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³ at room temperature. What are ne and nh?
steps: In an intrinsic semiconductor, ne = nh = ni
ne = 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³
nh = 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³

traps: Holes move along the field, electrons against it
Intrinsic conductivity increases, not decreases, with temperature

learn.hook: Add just one impurity atom per million silicon atoms and the conductivity jumps enormously. This deliberate 'impurity' is called doping.
points: Doping: adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity. The dopant atoms replace some Si or Ge atoms.

n-type: doping with a pentavalent element (arsenic As, phosphorus P, antimony Sb). Four electrons bond; the fifth is loosely held and easily freed. These donors give extra electrons, which are majority carriers; holes are minority carriers.
p-type: doping with a trivalent element (indium In, boron B, aluminium Al). One bond is incomplete, creating a hole. These acceptors give holes as majority carriers; electrons are minority carriers.

Band picture: donor levels lie just below the conduction band, so donated electrons easily jump up. Acceptor levels lie just above the valence band, so valence electrons easily jump into them, leaving holes.
A doped semiconductor as a whole remains electrically neutral.

example.q: Silicon is doped with phosphorus. What type of semiconductor results, and what are its majority carriers?
steps: Phosphorus is pentavalent (group 15).
Its fifth electron becomes free: a donor.
n-type, with electrons as majority carriers.

learn.reallife: The solar cells being made by Indian manufacturers in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu use phosphorus-doped (n-type) and boron-doped (p-type) silicon layers.

p-type: In, B, Al (acceptors); holes majority

topics.title: Carrier concentrations and the mass action law

learn.hook: Doping silicon with donors floods it with electrons, and something surprising happens: the number of holes drops dramatically.
points: Law of mass action: in thermal equilibrium, ne × nh = ni², for intrinsic and doped semiconductors alike.
In n-type material with donor density ND (all ionised): ne ≈ ND and nh = ni²/ND, which is far smaller.
In p-type material with acceptor density NA: nh ≈ NA and ne = ni²/NA.
Adding donors increases electrons and reduces holes, because extra electrons recombine with holes.

Problem tips: identify majority carriers from the dopant, use mass action for minority carriers, recall band gaps (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV), and remember a full-wave rectifier doubles the output frequency.

example.q: Silicon (ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped with 9 × 10²² m⁻³ arsenic atoms. Find ne and nh.
steps: Arsenic is a donor, so ne ≈ ND = 9 × 10²² m⁻³
nh = ni²/ne = (1.5 × 10¹⁶)²/(9 × 10²²)

revise.summary: In equilibrium the law of mass action ne × nh = ni² holds for intrinsic and doped semiconductors. In n-type ne ≈ ND and nh = ni²/ND; in p-type nh ≈ NA and ne = ni²/NA, so adding donors lowers the hole density.

Use ni², not ni, in mass action

learn.hook: Join p-type and n-type silicon and, in a microsecond, a thin barrier builds itself at the boundary. That barrier is what makes diodes, LEDs and solar cells work.
points: Formation: at the junction, electrons diffuse from the n-side (high concentration) to the p-side, and holes diffuse from p to n. This diffusion current flows from p to n.
Electrons leaving the n-side expose positive donor ions; holes leaving the p-side expose negative acceptor ions. These immobile ions form the depletion region, which has no free carriers.
The ions create an electric field (from n to p) that drives minority carriers across the junction: the drift current, opposite to diffusion current.
In equilibrium, diffusion current = drift current, so there is no net current.
The potential difference across the depletion region is the barrier potential: about 0.7 V for Si and 0.2 V for Ge (ignoring small variations).

example.q: Why is there no net current across an unbiased p-n junction?
steps: Diffusion of majority carriers gives a current from p to n.
The junction field drives a drift current of minority carriers from n to p.
In equilibrium the two are equal and opposite.
example.answer: Diffusion and drift currents balance each other

learn.reallife: Every LED street light installed under India's Street Lighting National Programme has a p-n junction at its heart.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is the depletion layer, and why is it there?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Majority carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving immobile ions with no free carriers; their field creates the barrier. Junction born!

revise.summary: At a p-n junction, majority carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving a depletion region of immobile ions whose field (n to p) drives a drift current of minority carriers. In equilibrium drift and diffusion balance, with a barrier potential of about 0.7 V (Si) or 0.2 V (Ge).
remember: Depletion region: immobile ions, no free carriers
traps: Don't swap them: drift is due to minority carriers, diffusion to majority carriers
An unbiased junction carries no net current

learn.hook: A diode is a one-way street for current. Push it the right way and current flows easily; push the wrong way and almost nothing gets through.
points: Diode symbol: an arrow (triangle) with a bar. The p-side is the anode, the n-side the cathode; the arrow shows the direction of conventional current in forward bias.

Forward bias: p connected to the positive terminal. The applied voltage opposes the barrier, the depletion layer narrows, and once V exceeds the threshold (cut-in or knee) voltage, about 0.7 V for Si and 0.2 V for Ge, current rises sharply (milliamperes).

Reverse bias: p connected to the negative terminal. The barrier rises, the depletion layer widens, and only a tiny reverse saturation current (microamperes) flows, due to minority carriers. It hardly changes with voltage.
Reverse breakdown: at a large reverse voltage the reverse current suddenly increases sharply.
So a diode conducts well in one direction only.

example.q: A silicon diode is connected with its p-side to the positive terminal of a 3 V battery through a resistor. Is it forward or reverse biased, and does it conduct?
steps: p-side to positive means forward bias.
3 V exceeds the cut-in voltage (~0.7 V).
So it conducts significantly.

learn.reallife: Phone chargers sold across India contain diodes that let current through only one way; that is how they turn the AC from the wall socket into the DC a battery needs.

learn.hook: Plot current against voltage for a diode and you get a curve that hugs zero, then shoots up like a hockey stick. Its slope tells you the diode's resistance.
points: Experiment: the diode is connected to a variable DC supply with a milliammeter and voltmeter for forward bias; for reverse bias, a microammeter is used and the supply reversed. Use a series resistor to protect the diode.
Forward characteristic: very small current up to the threshold voltage, then a steep, non-linear rise.
Reverse characteristic: a tiny, nearly constant current (µA) until breakdown.
Dynamic resistance rd = ΔV/ΔI, the inverse slope of the V-I curve at a point. It is small in forward bias above threshold and very large in reverse bias.
Lab safety: never exceed the diode's rated current; a small series resistor prevents overheating, and switch off before rewiring.

learn.reallife: Electronics labs in Indian polytechnics and engineering colleges still have students trace diode V-I curves by hand, a rite of passage for future engineers.

learn.hook: Your phone battery needs DC, but the socket gives AC. Inside the charger, diodes chop and flip the AC into one-way pulses, then a capacitor smooths them out.
points: Rectification: converting AC into DC using the one-way conduction of diodes.

Half-wave rectifier: one diode in series with the load. It conducts only in the half-cycles when it is forward biased, so the output is pulsating DC with alternate half-cycles missing. Output frequency = input frequency.
Full-wave rectifier: a centre-tap transformer with two diodes. Each diode conducts in alternate half-cycles, sending current through the load in the same direction both times.
The full-wave output has twice the input frequency (100 Hz for 50 Hz mains) and is more efficient.

Filter: a capacitor across the load (capacitor-input filter) charges during each peak and discharges slowly between peaks, smoothing the output. A larger C and larger load resistance RL give smaller ripple.

example.q: A full-wave rectifier works on 50 Hz mains. What is the output frequency, and why?
steps: Each half-cycle produces one output pulse.
There are 2 × 50 = 100 half-cycles per second.
So the output frequency is 100 Hz.

learn.reallife: The adaptors that power Wi-Fi routers and set-top boxes in Indian homes contain full-wave rectifiers with capacitor filters, turning 230 V, 50 Hz AC into steady low-voltage DC.
